co_pipeline.jd:
Brightquill Labs GmbH (fictional company) — Senior Analytics Engineer, Berlin (hybrid, 2 days office).

About us: Brightquill Labs builds route-optimisation software for mid-sized European parcel carriers. We serve 140 carriers across 9 countries and process about 30 million parcel events a day. Our data platform team is 11 people: 4 data engineers, 5 analytics engineers, 2 data product managers. We are a Series B company with roughly 260 employees.

The role: You will own the modelling layer between our raw event streams and every metric our carriers and our own commercial team see. Today that layer is a mix of hand-written SQL views, an older Airflow DAG estate and a young dbt project. Your first year is about consolidating it into one tested, documented dbt project on Snowflake, with clear ownership and SLAs per model.

What you will do: design and maintain dimensional models for parcels, routes, drivers, depots and invoices; define metric contracts with product and finance; write dbt tests and data-quality monitors; migrate legacy Airflow SQL into dbt; review pull requests from 4 other analytics engineers; partner with data engineers on ingestion contracts from Kafka; build the semantic layer that powers our customer-facing analytics in Looker; mentor two junior analytics engineers; run quarterly model-health reviews; write RFCs for significant modelling changes; take part in a light on-call rotation (business hours only) for data incidents.

Must have: 5+ years in analytics engineering or data analytics with strong SQL; production dbt experience including macros, incremental models and snapshots; a cloud warehouse (Snowflake preferred, BigQuery or Redshift fine); Git-based workflows and code review; experience defining metrics with business stakeholders; written English at C1 or above.

Nice to have: Looker/LookML; Python for data tooling; experience with event data at scale (10M+ rows per day); logistics or marketplace domain knowledge; German at B1 or above; experience leading a migration project end to end; familiarity with data contracts and schema registries.

How we work: small teams, written culture, RFCs before large changes, two-week cycles, no meetings on Wednesdays. We publish salary bands internally. Hybrid in Berlin with two office days. Relocation support available within the EU. We sponsor visas for non-EU candidates.

Compensation: EUR 78,000–92,000 base, plus virtual stock options (VSOP), 30 days holiday, EUR 1,500 learning budget, public transport ticket, and a home-office allowance.

Interview process: 30-minute recruiter call; 60-minute hiring manager conversation; take-home exercise (max 3 hours, paid at EUR 150) modelling a small parcel dataset in dbt; 90-minute panel with two analytics engineers and a product manager; 30-minute values conversation with a co-founder. We aim to complete the process in three weeks.

Our stack in detail: Snowflake (Enterprise), dbt Core 1.x running in GitHub Actions, Airflow 2 (being reduced), Kafka and Kafka Connect for ingestion, Fivetran for SaaS sources (Salesforce, HubSpot, Zendesk), Looker for internal and embedded analytics, Monte Carlo for observability, Terraform for warehouse permissions, and a small Python toolkit for data-quality checks. We use Linear for planning and Notion for documentation.

First 90 days: week 1–2 onboarding and shadowing the on-call rota; by day 30 you will have shipped your first model migration and reviewed the existing test coverage; by day 60 you will present an RFC for the target dbt project structure; by day 90 you will have migrated the parcel and route fact tables and agreed metric contracts for on-time delivery rate, cost per parcel and depot utilisation with product and finance.

Challenges you will face: legacy views with undocumented business logic; duplicated metric definitions across teams; late-arriving events from carrier scanners; time-zone handling across nine countries; customer requests for custom metrics that do not fit the shared model; and balancing migration work against new feature requests from the commercial team.

Diversity: we welcome applications from people of all backgrounds. If you need adjustments during the interview process, tell us and we will make them. Please do not include a photo or date of birth in your CV.

Additional context: carriers expect daily refreshed dashboards by 07:00 local time, and our service-level target for the core parcel models is 99.5% on-time freshness per month. Model owners write a short incident note for every breach.

blocks.roleSummary: Archetype: Analytics Engineer / BI Developer in title only. In practice this is legacy maintenance. Domain: insurance, actuarial reporting. Function: maintain COBOL-to-SQL migration scripts. Seniority: senior (8+ years COBOL). Remote: remote within Portugal, and the candidate must reside there. Team size: unknown. TL;DR: a mainframe COBOL maintenance job with an analytics-engineer title, requiring actuarial certification, Portuguese C2 and Portugal residency.
blocks.cvMatch:
Requirement-by-requirement mapping against the CV:
- 8+ years COBOL: nothing in the CV. No COBOL anywhere.
- Mainframe JCL: nothing in the CV.
- Actuarial certification (required): not in the CV. Education is "MSc Applied Statistics, Fictional University of Utrecht, 2016", which is not an actuarial credential.
- Portuguese C2 (required): not in the CV. Languages listed are English (C2), Dutch (B2), German (B1).
- Must reside in Portugal: the CV says Utrecht, Netherlands.
- COBOL-to-SQL migration scripts: the only adjacent line is "Automated claims reporting in SQL and Excel VBA" (Tidewater Insurance, 2016-2018). That is SQL reporting, not migration of legacy code.
What does overlap: SQL, and one junior-level insurance claims reporting role. The modern analytics-engineering stack in the CV ("Built a dbt + Snowflake semantic layer covering 42 core metrics", "190 dbt tests") is not used in this role.
blocks.levelStrategy: The JD asks for senior-level legacy depth (8+ years COBOL). The candidate's natural level for an Analytics Engineer role is senior, backed by "Lead Data Analyst" and "Led a team of 3 analysts". The problem is not level but domain: the seniority here is measured in COBOL and mainframe years the candidate does not have. Selling senior: there is no honest way to sell senior against this JD, because the senior criteria are the missing ones. Do not stretch the 2016-2018 SQL/VBA claims work into mainframe experience. If they downlevel you: not worth negotiating, because the scope (COBOL maintenance) and the pay both miss the target.
blocks.compResearch: JD location: Lisbon, Portugal. The JD states EUR 38,000. I have no live market data, so this is an estimate: I don't have a reliable static benchmark for senior analytics roles in Portugal, so treat the market range as unknown. What can be said safely: EUR 38,000 is well below the candidate's stated target of EUR 85,000 (less than half). It is also below the static senior Data Analyst references for other Western European markets (Netherlands EUR 55k-80k, Germany EUR 65k-85k), and the role asks for senior COBOL skills plus a professional actuarial certification, which are rare and normally priced higher. Verdict: clearly below target and likely below market for the requirements stated. I do not recommend pursuing this at this pay.
blocks.personalizationHook: No CV or hook changes recommended. Tailoring the CV toward COBOL or actuarial work would pull it away from the candidate's stated goal (ownership of the modelling layer) and would risk misrepresenting experience. If the candidate still wants to apply, the only honest hook is the "Tidewater Insurance" claims reporting line, and it is too thin to carry an application for a role requiring 8+ years of COBOL.
blocks.interviewPrep: Main risk: you would be screened out on the hard requirements before any interview (no COBOL, no JCL, no actuarial certification, no Portuguese, not resident in Portugal). Interview preparation is not worth the time. Prepare for roles where the dbt semantic layer and the 42-metric build are the lead story.

gaps.why: Core of the job. The CV shows none (SQL, dbt, Snowflake, Python only).
gaps.bridge: None that is honest. A short COBOL course would not close an 8-year gap. Do not claim it.

gaps.why: Stated as required. The CV has an MSc in Applied Statistics, which is not an actuarial qualification.
gaps.bridge: Only an actual actuarial credential would close this, which is a multi-year path and off the candidate's stated goal.

gaps.why: The CV lists English C2, Dutch B2, German B1 and no Portuguese.
gaps.bridge: None realistic in the hiring window.

gaps.why: The candidate is based in Utrecht, Netherlands, and the role is remote only within Portugal.
gaps.bridge: Only relocation would solve it, and that is not justified at EUR 38,000 against a EUR 85,000 target.

redFlagQuestions.question: Why does an "Analytics Engineer" role require 8+ years of COBOL?
redFlagQuestions.answer: The title does not match the work. This is legacy mainframe maintenance, not modern analytics engineering (no dbt, warehouse or semantic-layer work is mentioned). Ask what the target architecture is and whether any modern stack is planned. If the answer is no, the role will not build the skills in the candidate's target path.

redFlagQuestions.question: Is EUR 38,000 consistent with the senior requirements (8+ years COBOL plus actuarial certification)?
redFlagQuestions.answer: No. It is far below the candidate's EUR 85,000 target and looks low for a certified specialist profile. I'd only discuss it if comp were reset to a level that fits the requirements, and there is no sign of that.

co_stories.question: Tell me about a time you had to convince stakeholders to change how a metric was defined.
co_stories.situation: At Quokka Logistics BV, I was Lead Data Analyst building a dbt + Snowflake semantic layer for 42 core metrics. Reporting took about 3 days a week. Part of the cause was that teams defined shared metrics in their own ways. A single metric could carry different definitions depending on who reported it. (Note: the CV does not name the specific metric or the teams involved, so I describe the pattern in general terms. Add the real example before using this story.)
co_stories.task: I had to get stakeholders to agree on one definition per metric, so the semantic layer could be the single source of truth. That meant asking some teams to give up the definition they already used.
co_stories.action: I mapped how each metric was currently defined and showed where the numbers disagreed. I proposed one definition per metric and encoded it once in dbt. I protected it with data tests (the team now runs 190 dbt tests) and introduced code review, so any later definition change had to be visible and agreed. I led a team of 3 analysts through this work. [Add from your memory: who you pitched, what objections came up, and how you resolved them. The CV does not record these details.]
co_stories.result: The semantic layer now covers 42 core metrics. Weekly reporting effort dropped from 3 days to 4 hours. Metric definitions are now governed by reviewed code and tests, not by individual spreadsheets or dashboards.
co_stories.reflection: A metric definition is a business agreement first and a code problem second. The dbt model only holds if the people who own the number have signed off on it. Next time I would involve the metric owners earlier, before building, and write the definition and its edge cases in the model docs. That would shorten the debate and make the change stick. (Confirm this matches what you actually learned. Edit it if it does not.)
co_stories.fullStory: At Quokka Logistics, I led the build of a dbt + Snowflake semantic layer covering 42 core metrics. Weekly reporting took about 3 days, partly because teams defined shared metrics in different ways. My task was to get stakeholders to agree on one definition per metric, even when that meant some teams changed what they used. I mapped the existing definitions and showed where the numbers disagreed. Then I proposed a single definition for each and encoded it once in dbt. I added code review and data tests so definitions could only change in the open. Today 190 dbt tests guard the layer. Weekly reporting effort fell from 3 days to 4 hours. The lesson: a metric definition is a business agreement before it is a code problem. I would now bring metric owners in before building, and document each definition and its edge cases in the model.
